utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Josse, are you ready to continue the examination in chief of Mr. Milincic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Perhaps it would be practical that the parties inform the usher whether there are any procedural matters to be raised, so that we don't have to wait. Mr. Tieger, I don't know whether you heard me, but if the parties would inform the usher whether there are any procedural matters to be raised, because, if not, I would accept that the witness already enters the courtroom. Yes? And good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Milincic. If you put them on the top of your head, it's better. Mr. Milincic, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Josse will now continue to examine you. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, when we broke off yesterday I was asking you about Mr. Krajisnik. My next question is: Could you assess the popularity of Mr. Krajisnik in 1992 in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that we do not receive English translation on channel 4.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We now can hear you. And it does not appear on the transcript either. Mr. Milincic, would you please repeat your answer, because we didn't receive translation. So you were asked about -- you were asked about your assessment of the popularity of Mr. Krajisnik in 1992, in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is only my opinion, without any official indicators to support it. However, at parties or rallies in the street, I could hear them talking about the assembly sessions that were going on. Those were the first multi-party assembly sessions. This was something new for us. This was aired on TV. The way the power was divided was that the assembly went to the SDS, the government went to the Croats, the Presidency went to the Muslims. So tensions were expected to appear. However, Mr. Krajisnik showed a lot of perseverance to deal with all those novelties and this created a charisma attached to his personality. This is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And did the Srbac municipality ever receive any orders from Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what orders you are referring to. I don't know what to say to that. I don't remember any order having come from the president of the assembly to the president of the assembly of Srbac. This was just not regulated by the law. There were laws, however. There were old laws of the former Yugoslavia and the former Bosnia and Herzegovina that were in place, and we used them. I can't tell you something -- anything about any improvisations. I don't know of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I now want to move on to a different subject, please, and I want to ask you whether you ever attended -- I'm going to start again, if I may. Does the name Mirzet Karabeg, from Sanski Most, mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It does ring a bell, especially in connection with what I'm here for. I believe that he hailed from Sanski Most, and he was a member of the Executive Board. Maybe he was its president or just a board member.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He was the president at one point. That's right. Did you ever attend a meeting of the Bosanska Krajina region in March of 1991, the meeting taking place in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Banski Dvori. I believe that this was in December 1991, but I can't be sure of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The meeting I'm asking you about was in March of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And do you remember a meeting of that region which Mr. Karabeg attended?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time there were such meetings in Banja Luka. All the presidents of the Municipal Assemblies would gather there. At one of such meetings in Banski Dvori, before the agenda was adopted, a man got to his feet. That's when I first noticed him. And in hindsight, I remember that his debate differed from the debate of the others and that he left the meeting at the very beginning, him and another man. He had said before that that he had expected to hear something else at the assembly meeting, and his feeling was that the agenda that was about to be adopted differed from the agenda that was announced, that he was at the session of the assembly by chance, that he didn't want to attend the meeting, and he left the room. Later on, I heard who they were, that one of them was from Sanski Most and the other one from Prijedor. In other words, they did not stay at the meeting. People wanted to keep them, wanted them to stay, told them that things would be changed, that there were normally debates before the agenda was adopted, and then things calmed down. In other words, these two men left before the agenda was adopted and before the session actually started, and therefore, he never participated in the official part of the debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you subsequently learn the name of the man from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked who the man was and how come he had reacted in that way, and those who stayed in the room started discussing the case and they were sorry that the men did not stay. I only knew that they were from Sanski Most and Prijedor, respectively. And later on, after I was invited as a witness in this Court, I learnt what their names were, or what his name was. You asked me if I remember the event. Yes, I do remember the event, but at that time, I didn't know the man's name. It was only later on that I learned that the man's name was Karabeg and that he is from Sanski Most, and I also learned that the other man was from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How did you learn that the man's name was Karabeg from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody told me then. In the meantime, I forgot. And as I was preparing to testify, I asked what the man's name was, and I was told. Believe me, in a fortnight, I will again not be able to recall this person's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the meeting that you have just described, or indeed at any other meeting of the Bosanska Krajina region, do you remember a judge of the misdemeanour court of Srbac attending?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, when the Defence team of Mr. Krajisnik asked me if I had attended that meeting, I said of course I was, and then they asked me if I remember the words of a certain man and that he left the session. I said yes, but I don't remember his name. And then I was astonished by a story about that session, according to which there were discussions at the session about the work of the Serbian media being hindered and that the president of the court in Srbac proposed some taxes that would stop the work of all the non-Serb media. Obviously, as the only person who was there representing Srbac, and bearing in mind the fact that nobody ever attended such meetings from the court in Srbac, and if you know that the misdemeanours court president was a woman and that she was only revoked from her position only two months ago, which means that she had been the president of the court for 15 years before that. Her name is Biljana Lalovic and she is currently employed at the municipality. So if you're referring to the misdemeanours court president, it would be Biljana Lalovic, and she never attended any of those meetings. And if you are referring to the president of the municipal court, not the misdemeanours court but the municipal court, at that time, that was Ljubomir Sandic. Today he is a deputy in the Republican Assembly. At that time he belonged to a different party, to the Party of Socialists. Neither as a person, nor as a professional, would he have stated something like that. None of the presidents of the courts in Srbac ever attended the assembly session meetings. Srbac is a place where the inter-ethnic tensions could not be felt. They were equal to zero, if I may put it that way. The inhabitants of that place were Serbs. I mentioned the share of Muslims and Croats yesterday. And thirdly, Srbac is very close to the border with Croatia, and it did not have any possibility to stop the work of other media, either technical or financial possibilities. We are in the position to watch Croatian television because of the conflagration of the ground. It's flat all the way to Zagreb. Maybe that statement was issued by somebody from Srbac, but not at the assembly session. If you did a poll today in Srbac, people would remember that and people would tell you that this cannot be true, that this statement could not possibly be true, although it was attached to the president of the court in Srbac. And let me repeat that those sessions were never attended by anybody else but presidents of the municipal assemblies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The last topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just ask you one question, Mr. Josse. The question you just put to the witness, are they in any relation with any early evidence presented? Because then I'd like --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you -- I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I can give the page in the transcript, if needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you gave the date. Is it the Karabeg -- I have the date, but if you look at the word "court," you'll find a lot of courts, but mainly this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As usual, Mr. Tieger is better organised than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not at all. In this case, Your Honour, and it's a point I wanted to raise. In fairness to Mr. Josse, there was a passing exchange between the two of us about this matter, a matter that was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Put to that witness. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- raised in 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understood that it was a matter the Defence was considering and believed that I would be advised if evidence along these lines was going to be led. I fully accept that was a misunderstanding. However, it leaves me in an awkward and difficult position. I raise that for a couple of reasons. Number 1, I think that it highlights the importance of the detail of 65 ters and secondly, although I don't anticipate at this point that I will seek to defer my cross-examination for this reason, I do want to reserve this particular issue by noting it at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just help, Your Honour? It's page -- because I've got it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem is that in my LiveNote system the pages are by the day and not numbered through. But if you would have a specific sequence of words, it will be no problem for me to find it. But unfortunately, the word "court" is not very helpful, because you very often address a court, which is a different court. The word "judge" doesn't help that much, because there are three Judges here who are addressed frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Misdemeanours court? That's what I used that expression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say the "misdemeanours" appears, then I'll be able to find it, at least if I know how to write "misdemeanours" - yes, please - without spelling mistakes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For what it's worth, Your Honour, I take on board what my learned friend Mr. Tieger has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And apart from that, could you give me the date? Was it the 25th of May or was it -- or don't you know? I'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I've only got the transcript page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll find it. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The last topic that I want to ask you about, Mr. Milincic, relates to the Main Board of the SDS. Did you attend meetings of the Main Board in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How many meetings did you go to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven or eight. There was normally one meeting a month, sometimes every six weeks. I certainly didn't attend more than eight meetings in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what about 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The work of the party was frozen at the time and we turned to the problems prevailing in our respective municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In 1991, the meetings you attended, did Mr. Krajisnik attend at some or all of them, any of them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the SDS meeting at Holiday Inn on the 12th or the 14th July, 1991 - I said that yesterday - Mr. Krajisnik was either accepted as a member of the party or became a member of the Main Board, either one or the other, when he attended the meeting of the SDS party. There were a few more meetings in the course of that year. He would not stay until the end, or he would come late, because of his previous commitments. I don't have a clear recollection of that. It's very difficult for me to be sure of any of this. It was a long time ago, and I didn't find it that significant at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you attend a meeting at the Holiday Inn in December?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The previous point may have been -- the previous issue may have been the subject of a misunderstanding, but it's clear to me now, and I believe to the Court, what evidence Defence is seeking to elicit now and it's frankly a bit astonishing to me that that appears nowhere in the 65 ter, nor does, in general, the line of questioning that the Defence has just been pursuing. And I think if -- we've been expressing our concerns about this throughout. There -- I don't need to belabour the point. I think that stands for itself. I'm not entirely sure what remedy at this moment I would suggest, but this is inappropriate and we need to address it, and it does leave me in an inappropriately unprepared position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse -- but perhaps before I give you an opportunity. You said you do not know what remedy to suggest at this moment. Which options did you have in mind, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, clearly, one of the options would be -- here are some options that occur to me. We could lead the evidence and defer the cross-examination on that point; we could lead the evidence and defer the cross-examination in toto until a later point; the Court could exclude evidence that was not properly noticed. Again, I'm not urging one or another at this point. I'm simply identifying alternatives that come to mind immediately. I don't want to urge upon the Court any measures harsher or more Draconian than necessary, but must insist that the function of the summaries be recognised and complied with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, before you continue, would you please respond to Mr. Tieger's concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't really, with respect, accept my learned friend's criticism in this regard. Your Honour, the last matter, he has an absolute, justified point about. There is no way he could possibly know that I was going to ask this witness about Mr. Karabeg's evidence unless he had some advance notice. But to take that point in relation to what I'm about to ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last question, you mean in relation to the last question about the meeting later that year?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely. And my learned friend is right. Of course he knows where it's going. It's relevant, it's the central issue, or one of the most central issues in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it appear on the 65 ter?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It says -- the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Membership. Membership. Let's try to deal with it in a way that -- yes. Well, we know that he's a member now, isn't it? He testified about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the fact that he's a member is in the 65 ter. It's the next point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you consider 65 ter summaries sufficiently detailed, if whatever happened during the membership of a certain body, that everything that happened in that body would be covered by it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, no, but the particular event I'm about to ask about, which is so central to this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- I submit, does not need to be in each and every 65 ter. That's really the point I'm contending on behalf of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is inclined to take the initiative itself, if it's clear to everyone where we are going and where the Chamber does agree that merely mentioning membership is not sufficient for a 65 ter, let's see what the witness may know about what everyone seems to understand to be an important issue in this case. So we might first put a few questions to the witness and then see whether you have any additional questions, Mr. Josse. Mr. Milincic, about meetings of the Main Board, do you remember any other meetings you attended in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not receive translation at this moment. Could the interpreters -- there seems to be a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear us now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: So the witness said: Those were only the meetings of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say "those were the only meetings," that's the July meeting. And what was the other meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Josse asked whether I attended a meeting in December, and I said yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That answer does not appear on the transcript, so therefore, I was -- I saw it in the question, but I didn't -- so you attended a meeting in December. Could you tell us where that meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have said yes, although I'm not sure, but I don't want to be argumentative. But as a member of the SDS and the Presidency in Srbac, I tried to attend as many meetings as I possibly could, although I can't remember very clearly. I nevertheless say yes, they were at the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you by any chance remember the date of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it at the beginning of December?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was in December, in winter, because we have a long way to travel, and so we tend to have problems with transport and all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you describe us who were present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Members of the Main Board. I think there were 45 members. The president of the party, Mr. Karadzic, I can't say -- presumably, people from the government, but who exactly and how many of them, since we at that time had a joint government with the authorities at the BH level, I don't know who was there. I know that it was chaired by Mr. Karadzic. That's certain. But other than that, I'm not certain. I know I attended meetings, but as to everything else -- and I know we did have a quorum, so that meant that all members, 45 or 40, or at least 38, must be in there, because we did have a quorum. And we never left the meeting without doing any work. The session would be held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You earlier said that at the July meeting Mr. Krajisnik became a member of the party or became a member of the Main Board. That's the same what you said yesterday. So therefore, it's unclear if you say the members of the Main Board were there, whether this would include Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... whether you remember his presence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember, but I tend to think that he was, rather than that he wasn't. But I'm not sure. It is only logical that you want to hear the facts. I think he might have been, but I had no reason to keep it in mind, to try and remember who was there. I know I went, but other than that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, do you remember what happened during this meeting? I mean, what were the discussions about? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have to help me out, because I just can't do it like this. I mean, at those meetings, different things were being discussed, sowing, harvesting, media, politics, all kinds of things. So it would be interesting to specify the particular topic that you are interested in, because there were really wide-ranging topics. People are asked about everything, maybe various rulings, whether we could exert any influence upon that, and then granting loans, finding jobs for people, business-related matters, if a company was in trouble, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you receive an agenda in advance of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Presumably, but we got those agendas only very rarely. I suppose we got it once we arrived at the meeting. But I can't remember ever receiving a copy of the agenda in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say the agenda was distributed most probably during that meeting. Were there any other documents distributed during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure. I can't remember, and I wouldn't like to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not specifically related to this meeting, but usually, during those meetings, were documents distributed that came from the central organs of the party? Was that a common thing to happen? So I'm not talking specifically about the December meeting, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It happened sometimes. We did not have a clearly defined set of rules, and we discussed a number of different issues. So what we used to do was, either before or after these sessions, to have a kind of brainstorming session at the municipality level and discuss that with the president of the party. And, as I said, since Srbac had least problems, either in terms of the economy or ethnic problems, I was the least encouraged person to ask questions. There was nothing I needed to do. If there were any documents or any materials that we received, I would leave it up to the party to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was whether you usually received such kind of documents. Your answer was more what you did with these kind of documents. But was that a common thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I did, yes. When I received anything that was addressed to the municipality of Srbac, I would take it and take it to Srbac with me. As to whether all the documents and all the materials were identical, I do not know. But in as far as Srbac was concerned, I was given those materials and I would forward them to the party structure. The functioning of the local communities and boards, the municipal board, and suchlike. That was this party politics, as it were. But Srbac was in a rather special position from that point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You specifically said that you did not know whether the materials were identical. Could you explain to us what you had in mind when you said this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know what you're interested in, this Variant A and B. I've heard of that. But I'm claiming upon my full responsibility and I'm willing to suffer any consequences. But myself and Srbac never took part in any of these variants and we never received any documentations about Variants A, B, or C. I heard this when I talked to the lawyers. They mentioned these Variants A, B, C, did you see that, did you hear about this ethnic cleansing and all that? But the thing is, I needed to bring Croats and Muslims into Srbac in order to calm things down amongst the Serbs. And as to these Variants A and B, if they were about ethnic cleansing or whatever, I never had anything to do with it. I'm here before the Court and I know what you're after. I've heard of it now, but I'm claiming upon my full responsibility that the president of the SDS in Srbac and the member of the full board, that is to say, myself, had never set eyes on this. Maybe this was being kept from me. I don't know whether another municipality may have received these documents. I do not know. But certainly I never saw anything like that in Srbac. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you say for that reason that you do not know whether it was identical, the material?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of any document being distributed to one municipality in a different form or in a different copy, compared to the document given to another municipality? You understand what I mean? Are you aware of -- that it ever happened that two different copies of a document concerning the same matter were distributed to the various representatives of the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're making yourself very clear. I do see what your direct question is. But I'm not in a position to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A similar question, Witness. During these meetings, can you tell us that the municipalities received a sort of general instructions that were applicable to all municipalities? Did that ever happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were discussions, fears that were being voiced, assumptions, along the lines: What if there is a war? Are we going to be protected, and if so, in what way, and how should we get supplies, how should we organise the defence? So it was some kind of preliminary discussion. But since we were not threatened in Srbac -- I didn't participate in any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Sorry. Please answer my question, Witness. During these types of meetings, did it ever happen that you received from the Main Board, from the central body, did you ever receive general circulars applicable to all municipalities. In other words, instructions that all municipalities, each and every municipality, were bound to apply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember that, and I'm really curious to check whether this exists anywhere in the SDS archives in Srbac. Because I really do not remember that. And I believe that, had I received something like that, it would have been debated at the Municipal Board of the SDS in Srbac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But have you ever received that type of documents addressed to all the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that some statutory matters and party questions, some documents I did bring back to Srbac and circulate, but this sort of material, such a weighty document, if you see what I mean, is not something that I ever saw. And I said that in case it does exist, I'm really curious to see it. And had it existed at the time, we would have certainly debated it. Or rather, had I even received it, it would have had no impact whatsoever, because there was just no relevance, from my point of view, and it would have been doomed to oblivion. But no, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry, but I'm not satisfied with your answer. So we'll just go on very calmly. I would like you to understand my question. I would like my question to be very clear to you. During these meetings, these types of meetings, did the Main Board, the main body, did they distribute or circulate instructions to all representatives of all municipalities for these instructions to be implemented? I'm not talking about Variant A or B. I'm talking in general. I'm talking about any type of subject. Did the Main Board, and was the Main Board in a position to circulate instructions that were to be implemented by each and every one of the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm really sorry, but I cannot confirm that. No matter what the content, whatever I did receive, I forwarded to my own Municipal Board and the administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That ends my examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It looks as if it ends our examination, but ... No, I do understand. The subject has been covered. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour. If the Court will give me one minute to organise my materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, I hardly dare to say whether you're organised, but you are generally. But are you sufficiently organised to start?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Milincic. The other day you were asked by Judge Hanoteau about what you heard concerning what was happening in the surrounding, in the neighbouring municipalities, what sort of tension or violence, what you heard about what was happening. And you explained briefly to the Judge that you heard all manner of stories concerning other municipalities, although, you said: "In the midst of all this evil, I believe that Srbac managed to keep the evil at a very minor scale." I'd like to pursue that a bit, and I'd like more detail, please, on what you heard, what you learned about what was happening in the municipalities in the Krajina, and, specifically, what was happening to Muslims and Croats in the surrounding municipalities, in the Krajina municipalities, in the spring and summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I won't have much to say here. I told you that my primary task was Srbac, and as for the rumours, I heard strange and fantastic rumours about myself. At my expense, and as a person who has studied literature and psychologist, I know what the function of rumours is. And I remember a very clever German who said --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, please. I'm not asking about your educational background. I didn't ask you what you heard about yourself. I asked you what you were hearing about what was happening to the Muslims and Croats in the Krajina municipalities in the spring and summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard similar stories about the Serbs, Muslims, and Croats alike, about the conflict that had already started or is at the doorstep, in different municipalities, in different regions, starting with provocations, attacks on families, electricity outages, a pig that had been slaughtered and thrown in front of somebody's house, and that person was a Muslim. Those were stories and rumours. Those were threats. Phone harassment while telephone lines were still working. This was the psychology of fear, the fear that had already started spreading around us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's try to be clear on this. So do you want the Judges to understand that in 1992, all you knew about what was happening to Muslims and Croats in the Krajina municipalities was that there were some electricity outages, a pig had been slaughtered and thrown in front of someone's house, attacks on families, some provocations? That's your answer to the question? That's what you want the Judges to believe you understood occurred in 1992 to the Muslims and Croats of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, or some other detail for which I was neither responsible or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. had the power to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, no one asked you to tell us on matters you were responsible for. The question simply was: What did you learn at that time from others as to what happened in the Krajina to Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have to know that those things were not in the open; they were not public; that if some things had been happening, as you imply they were, this was not announced, this was not made public, and it was not made known in Srbac. I could listen to the media, which was already biased, and I could listen to the stories, but I was not in the centre of all these developments. Some information reached me with a delay of six months, about some crime, killing, violence, people being fired from work, but it happened on all the three sides. It depended on the municipality. It is only normal that I knew more about the Serbs and what was happening to them. But I also could not avoid hearing what was happening to the Muslims and the Croats, and especially bearing in mind the fact that later on I established contacts with some Croats, for example, Bishop Komarica, who was very communicative, very courageous, very energetic when it came to the status of Croats in the Krajina. He wanted to have that issue resolved in the safest possible manner. So I really can't provide you with a lot of information in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, you're not invited to provide a lot of information. If you say, "I could not avoid hearing what was happening to the Muslims and the Croats," Mr. Tieger just wants to know what you heard about them. Whether you were responsible is not important, whether it was official knowledge is not important, whether you know a lot or less or more. Just tell Mr. Tieger what you heard about what happened. That's the question, quite simple. And you spent now approximately 20, 25, 30 lines by not giving an answer to the question. Please tell him what you heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just told you. If an area was ethnically mixed, then Serbs and Muslims would confront each other, but it depended on the area. There were places where it was the Muslims who were victims; in the others, it was the Serbs who were victims. Please, do not insist on that, because I cannot give you a direct answer. I cannot say that things were either black or white, because I'm just not in a position to do that, because I don't know. You have not specified too clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, again, if you're asked what you heard about what happened to the Muslims and the Croats, someone might ask you after that, "And what did you hear about the Serbs?" You're not invited to strike a balance and to say that it was more that happened to the ones -- I'll ask you at a later stage to tell me what you heard about the Serbs. But please answer now Mr. Tieger's question. You say there were places where it was that the Muslims who were victims. Victims of what, did you hear they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Victims of violence. Please, don't ask me to explain what violence is. When somebody is beaten or when one is chased out of their house. I expect from you to start asking me about the year 1995. Then I will be in a position to provide you with facts that will also provide an answer to your question. When we start talking about the fall of AR Krajina and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, I'm going to stop you. You don't have to tell Mr. Tieger what he should ask you. Let's be quite clear. You heard about violence. You said "don't ask me." Did you hear about people being killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard comments. I listened to stories. But nothing was official.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking whether -- I said before, it doesn't matter whether it's official or not. Did you hear about persons being killed, Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I can't give you an answer as directly as you would want me to. I cannot establish a link between a place and a person or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- or maybe Gradiska, Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, again, the only thing I'm asking you, whether you heard that Muslims and Croats were killed. I'm not asking whether you knew whether they told you where and when and how many; might the following questions. Did you hear about Muslims and Croats --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard. I heard. I heard. I heard. But I'm trying to be specific and tell you about a place. But I can't. I heard stories. I heard rumours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one asks you at this moment to tell us about places. Did you hear about members of the civilian population being rounded up and detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that people were ill-treated. I don't know any of the details. I don't know whether they were detained, whether they were sent to work or whether they were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed. May I instruct you, Mr. Milincic, just to answer the questions. I do understand that you want to give a full, balanced picture of what you know. Please be aware that this Chamber hears a lot of evidence and that if there are important matters you would like to add to that what has been asked to you, you always could address me at a later stage and say, "I'd like to add something," and then we'll give you an opportunity to do so. But start by answering the questions. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, did I hear a suggestion from you that part of the reason you were unable to answer the questions was because you were simply isolated in Prnjavor and only concerned about Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Srbac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Srbac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Srbac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In hindsight, it's very difficult for me to say that I -- Srbac, Srbac, that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was interested in Srbac only.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I wanted to know if I understood you correctly to be saying that you didn't know -- you couldn't answer my earlier questions completely because you were just focussed on and isolated in Srbac.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please provide you with a comment here at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I'm actually not interested in the comment. Not before I get an answer to my question: Is that what you were trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I was interested in Srbac. That was my priority. And we started jealously keeping from each other our problems and the ways we tried to deal with our problems. And when I said "we," I'm referring to the various municipalities. I was afraid that, given that I didn't have any problems, any inter-ethnic problems or violence, that somebody would want to cause them, and unfortunately it did happen on three occasions. There were attempts to drag Srbac into a war area. That's why we kept our problems hidden from each other. You may not be convinced, but that was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You did interact with representatives, Serb representatives, of other municipalities in 1992, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, in fact, although you didn't mention it during the course of your examination-in-chief, you were involved in and a member of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the duration of it, a few months or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region of the Krajina was formed, the presidents of municipalities were also members and you attended some of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you had ample opportunity to learn from the leadership of the region and the leaders of other municipalities what was happening to people, and specifically what was happening to Muslims and Croats throughout the Krajina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you think that such a meeting is a forum where people would openly say what was going on? I did not have such information. I was not provided with such information at the Crisis Staff of the AR Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do I think that at such a meeting people would openly discuss what was going on? Let's look at a couple of those meetings, then. First of all, I noticed yesterday that on the list of SDS candidates for Srbac, you were number 2, I believe, and Vojo Kupresanin was number 4; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you know Vojo Kupresanin right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And he became president of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was his position?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you had the Court -- you had the opportunity periodically during the course of 1992 and 1993 to interact with Mr. Kupresanin, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me just turn quickly, then, to a couple of Mr. Kupresanin's comments at some of these meetings. First of all, if we could look to some comments at the 24th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, held in January of 1993, and I think that's tab 3. Mr. Kupresanin's comments begin in the English version at page 64, and in the B/C/S at page 18, which is 02149922. So you'll see two things there, Mr. Milincic, to identify the page at which Mr. Kupresanin's comments appear, first page 18 is listed -- that's because the -- this is broken down into two parts, but maybe easier for you, the heading 02149922. I see you reading, so it appears that you found it; is that right? And let me direct your attention in particular to his remarks found at page 19 in the B/C/S, the third paragraph. And at the bottom of page 65 of the English. Mr. Kupresanin said, after a longer discussion: "We say that the war was not necessary in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The war in Bosnia and Herzegovina was necessary. Right now, if we were to count the population right now, there would be," either "over" or "about," depending on whether it's "preko" or "eko" [phoen], "there would be over a million Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bosnia and Herzegovina would be predominantly a Serbian republic. Is war necessary in Serbia? It's a horrible thing to say that the war would be necessary in Serbia. If Serbia does not go into the war now, then in three to five years, the Albanians and Muslims will entirely legally overtake the power in Belgrade, along with the Serb opposition. This war Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was necessary for the Serb people." Mr. Milincic, isn't Mr. Kupresanin in that body, before all those delegates, acknowledging the reduction of the Muslim population in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a reduction that took place through massive forcible expulsions? Isn't that what that's a reference to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this is not the first time you've seen this, by the way, because you were present at that session, isn't that right? If you just turn a few pages along, perhaps your memory will be refreshed about your presence.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just want to turn to -- okay. You were present; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But I'm trying to see what it was that I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's okay. We'll turn back to that and I'll give you an opportunity to look at it, but I want to continue looking at Mr. Kupresanin's remarks, if we can, please. So in that connection, I'd like you to turn your attention to the 17th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, held in July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's an exhibit we've referred to repeatedly, so perhaps the best thing I can do at this point, since I don't think we have the extracts here for you, is simply to slowly repeat what was said there. It's been addressed in Court before, most recently with a witness I think -- well, I'm not going to particularly identify it, but I think if I use the expedient of just identifying the portion, I don't expect that the Defence will have any difficulties with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's see how it goes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. So you may proceed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, if necessary, I can produce some extracts of this session for you, but I think you'll be able to understand the gist of what is said via the translation. Now, the July -- the 17th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, as you can tell from the date in July of 1992, occurred at the height of the summer and after some period of time from the onset of the conflict. Mr. Kupresanin was present at that session, and, immediately before he spoke, Mr. Nedic spoke. And he said: "I am against solving the situation in Bosnia in haste. We must admit that the Muslims have been planted to us as a people whose executioners we are to be. I do not want the Serb people to be executioners, but I am also against us giving up our state, our land, and our territory." Mr. Kupresanin was also there, as I mentioned the fact he was the next speaker, and then subsequently Dr. Karadzic spoke. And after describing the -- his view of the Oriental mentality stemming from Islam, after noting the concern that the Serbs could not control the Muslim birth rate "since in five to six years, Muslims would make 51 per cent of the population of inner Bosnia," he went on to say: "There is truth in what Mr. Kupresanin has said," although, as I indicated, I think that was Mr. Nedic, "Although nobody in Europe will say it openly," he continued, "that this conflict was roused in order to eliminate the Muslims." And again, Mr. Milincic, at this session, at this meeting of Bosnian Serb leaders, republic, regional, municipal, wasn't this again an acknowledgment of what was happening to Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina in May, June, and July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I am reading this, and as I'm listening to you, memories come back. But in Srbac, we ignored this. We simply deleted this. This may be the fact, but now, if you're asking me to remember what was said 12 years ago, it is impossible. And I adhere to what I said before, that all the things that followed the inflammatory speeches and the concrete things that were happening in the life, I was standing firmly on the ground with my two feet and I made sure that life was normal in Srbac. Later on, the assembly was -- stopped working and everybody had to look after themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we'll turn after the break to what was happening in Srbac. But isn't it more fair to say, in retrospect, Mr. Milincic, that rather than standing firmly with your feet on the ground, that you were standing in Srbac, at best, with your eyes closed and your ears closed and ignoring everything that was happening to the Muslims and Croats in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What else could we do? In Srbac, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm moving to another topic, I believe, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's close to the time for a break. I think we would then have a break until 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, yesterday you discussed the killing of Mr. Halid Hadziselimovic. That was -- and you brought with you documents that you had sought out in Srbac. Now, that was one of the matters, if I understood you correctly, that you wanted to bring to the attention of the Court to dispel any misimpressions it might have about what happened in Srbac, to show what happened in Srbac; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what you wanted to show the Court was that in that instance in particular, a prominent and well-regarded Muslim had been murdered and the Serbian authorities had responded by prosecuting and imprisoning the perpetrator for that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you brought with you some documents to show that. Now, I noted with respect to some of the municipality documents, for example, that they weren't necessarily sequential, that you only brought, for example, some of the documents from the Srbac Official Gazette and some of the decisions that were made by the Municipal Assembly or Crisis Staff; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have brought some. I haven't brought quite a lot of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And with respect to the documents you brought with you concerning the murder of Mr. Hadziselimovic, the Court in particular asked you how it could know which murder those documents referred to, because it didn't seem clear on its face, and you assured the Court that it referred to the murder of Mr. Hadziselimovic because you knew how important it was to be accurate here and bring accurate information to the Court; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Mr. Milincic, we have found additional documents related to these particular documents, and I'd like to go through those with you now and with the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I'd like to turn to tab 15, which is a Banja Luka military court judgement in the case of Ljubomir Stankovic. And if we could, in addition to these documents, if the witness could also have tab 12 of the documents he brought with him and that were presented to the Court yesterday. And I trust that the Court also has those on hand, because I'll be referring to those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the translated tab 12 documents? I received in English some translations. I do not know whether this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I think those are entirely unrelated, Your Honour, if I understand it correctly. Those were translations related to another witness that the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think, as a matter of fact, I received something. I haven't got tab 12 with me handwritten "44" on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Forgive me. I should have referred to it by the specific exhibit number, which I understand is 100.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, no, now I've seen it, but ... I have a document in front of me, at least translation, handwritten 56, it says at the top. Yes. Mr. Registrar, we got from you ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That comes from the Prosecution. First let's deal with it and see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. Now I understand, Your Honour. I apologise for that. These are additional, related documents that may come up during the course of this examination, but I think for the time being they need not be given a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I may ask: Did Prosecution tab 15 -- was that given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, not yet. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P987, Your Honours, and the English translation, 987.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, because we're looking at two different documents, let's begin by moving through them fairly slowly and identifying them. Looking at the documents you brought with you yesterday, Defence Exhibit 100, you indicated that that was a judgement against Ljubomir Stankovic, and the -- as indicated on the document, or at one page of the document, it was a judgement dated April 20th, 1995, and the judgement number was 23/92. That's correct, isn't it? I'm reading from both the document and cross-referencing to your testimony of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Based on this, what I can see here, I can also tell what the subject of this judgement was. I received this from the police station in Srbac when I set off for The Hague, because I believe that this judgement referred to the killing of Halid Hadziselimovic. But here I see another murder appearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's move through that slowly, if we can. So first of all, I think we can agree, then, that Prosecution 987, the document which is a Banja Luka lower military court -- military prosecutor's office document, refers to the same matter. It's a judgement of 20 April 1995, and the number, again, is identical, 1K 23/92. So the documents you brought, you will agree, Mr. Milincic, refer to this judgement; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, it is correct, as you indicated yesterday, that this is a judgement; both exhibits reflect a judgement against Mr. Stankovic. But the story of Mr. Stankovic's crimes and subsequent prosecution is considerably different than the one you described yesterday. So if we could turn first to page 3 of the English, which should be page 2 of the B/C/S in front of you. Excuse me. It actually begins at the bottom if page 1, I think. It indicates the following, that at about 6.30 in the evening on August 7th, 1992, Mr. Stankovic, after a brief argument with Hasima Huskic, a 60-year-old woman, as the judgement later indicates, shot her at close range with his light machine-gun, with the intention of killing her, and she died. 15 minutes later, moving on further down the street, he fired his weapon at Hamza Bojadzic, who was sitting in front of his house, and in doing so, inflicted serious injuries to Mr. Bojadzic. 15 minutes after that, he entered the yard of Kasib Alagic and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. house Reuf Alagic with the same weapon and killed him. And then, on the same day, in the same yard, he fired the same weapon at Mr. Alagic's mother and seriously injured her. Now, that all occurred, Mr. Milincic, in the municipality of Srbac. You must remember that incident, four people gunned down, two of whom died. Surely you were aware of that and when it happened; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, and this person was somewhat problematic, that he was a member of the army. The police arrested him. He was convicted. But I was convinced that this trial was also for the murder of Halid Hadziselimovic. I just did not have all the information about the event and the outcome of this event. The police and the army had taken the matter in their hands. These are the facts, and I'm not denying them. I'm not saying that this is not how things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's take it one step at a time. First of all, this was -- was this a significant enough event in Srbac for it to come to your attention, or was the shooting of four Muslims and the death of two not sufficiently significant in the municipality of 20.000 people to be brought to the attention of the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A significant event that was given to the police and the army to deal with. The president of the municipality is a civilian. A husband and a wife were killed in the same municipality and they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My only question, Mr. Milincic, is whether or not you knew about this at the time it happened.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This did happen. I was informed, and I asked the enforcement agencies to do their best to prevent this person from doing even more harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you were actually involved with it and you specifically, according to you, asked that Mr. -- something be done about Mr. Stankovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked. I did not order. I could not issue any orders. I asked the people in the police and the army to deal with such matters as quickly as possible, to put these people on trial. I asked the police unit to deal with that. What could we do? He was on leave from the army. He brought his weapons and he caused problems. These people who were on leave, with weapons, this is what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You know, for the moment, Mr. Milincic, I'm trying to focus on what you knew and when you knew it. Well, on page 7 of this judgement, which would be, I believe, page 4 of the B/C/S, it turns out that Mr. Stankovic tried to raise a number of defences to his -- for -- and explanations for his killing of these two people and shooting of the others. And one of those defences, Mr. Milincic, as you can see, was that he was -- that his mind was still blurred by an earlier incident before this war, when a certain Halid Hadziselimovic attempted to kill him. But nothing happened as a result of that incident. It actually says no criminal proceedings were brought against Mr. Hadziselimovic because of his subsequent death. Mr. Milincic, Mr. Hadziselimovic was killed by Mr. Stankovic before this incident; isn't that right, in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't ask me to say anything about that. I am not Stankovic's lawyer. I'm not a judge. I don't know how things went. Neither the military court, nor any court, is obliged to inform the president of the municipality of how things went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're giving speeches. You're telling Mr. Tieger what he should not ask you. You're telling us what the or what are not the obligations of a military court. The question was simply whether it's right or not that Mr. Hadziselimovic was killed before that incident by Mr. Stankovic in May 1992. Either you know any of these facts, such as when he was killed, whether he was killed by Mr. Stankovic, and whether it was -- or you don't know. If you know, tell Mr. Tieger. If you don't know, tell him that you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know the sequence of these events. I don't know what preceded what and what followed what. I'm a bit nervous and now I feel guilty for something that was -- I was powerless about, that was beyond my authority. All of a sudden it seems I am guilty of a murder of somebody who was killed somewhere in a village, I don't know where. An armed person came and committed a crime, and I was the president of that municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, again, no one accuses you of being responsible for that killing. If you feel guilty, the only thing on which you might feel guilty, with some reason, is that you bring documents; if you would have read them, you would have known that they do not -- or at least that they do not present, on face value, what you said they presented. And now it turns out that you used them to support matters of which it now turns out that you had no sufficient knowledge to use them as support for that. So if you -- if there's any reason to feel guilty, is that you're playing the role of a messenger rather than the role of a witness who should tell what he knows for sure. If he has any doubt, he should say so. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So if I understood your answer correctly, Mr. Milincic, you knew that Mr. Stankovic killed Mr. Hadziselimovic, you knew that Mr. Stankovic killed Mr. Zukanovic - or Ms. Zukanovic, excuse me - Mr. Bojadzic, Mr. Alagic, and wounded Ms. -- Mr. Alagic, excuse me - wounded two people, killed two people, in 1992. So you knew about those incidents, were informed about them, indeed, according to you, made efforts to ensure that Mr. Stankovic was prosecuted for it, but you cannot now recall the sequence. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes. Yes, that's correct. Your interpretation is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, it must have come as quite a shock to you when -- let me ask you this question: Do you accept my representation, based upon the Banja Luka military court record of October 21st, 1993, page 3, that the incident involving Mr. Hadziselimovic and Mr. Stankovic occurred in late May 1992? I'm looking at a different document. You're welcome to see it. But I'm just asking for purposes of this examination whether you'll accept my representation that that was the date indicated, late May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as you sit here now, that's consistent with your recollection of approximately when Mr. Hadziselimovic was murdered?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you what information I had yesterday. Yesterday I told you what I know about Mr. Hadziselimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What I'm wondering, Mr. Milincic, is this: Is how it slipped your memory that a few months after killing perhaps the most prominent and, according to you, one of the well-liked members of the Muslim community in Srbac, Mr. Stankovic could then go on a killing and shooting spree which was brought to your attention, and you don't recall that, didn't -- don't remember that somehow he had been left free, after killing Mr. Hadziselimovic, to kill more Muslims. How did you forget that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of tragedies in Srbac. I believe that the Stankovic story had been over when he was arrested and incarcerated, but he was let go by the court and he committed more crimes. I really did not put the two in the same time frame or the same context. And this was not my conscious doing. It was unconscious on my part. I really don't remember the details, what preceded what. Stankovic was not my only problem. And as the president of the Municipal Assembly, I was powerless. I was a civilian. There was the police and there was the army. The two of them were supposed to deal with such things. I believe you when you describe things in the way you do, but at that moment the president of the municipality could not do anything if somebody was released by the army. I am -- I have -- I've forgotten what preceded what, what came first, what came next. Hadziselimovic I knew personally, and that's why I paid more attention to him. It may not be fair of me to -- not to pay so much attention to the others who were also victims. I'm saying this for the sake of those who are now listening to me, the Bosniaks in Srbac who are listening to me. I can fool you, but I cannot fool them, really. I apologise for saying this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question. May I just first comment. You're giving information to this Court primarily, so that's what should be on your mind. And it's a public hearing, so others will be able to follow it. But that's your first responsibility. Judge Hanoteau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you just said: [In English] "There were a lot of tragedies in Srbac." [Interpretation] Whereas yesterday I thought you said that Srbac was one of the communities that had not so many tragedies, that this community was spared from all these tragedies. Isn't that what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Srbac, we buried two fighters who had been decapitated. That was a tragedy for Srbac. We also had another murder where Serbs were killed by Serbs. We had a few attacks on the Serbian families, again, by other Serbs. Their nails were pulled out by pliers. They were tied, they were beaten to death, all in an attempt to extract money from them. There were killings by the Muslims, by Serbs. We had passersby through Serbs, we had checkpoints. Some military passed through Srbac, units, brigades, and they caused trouble in Srbac. I really can't remember as I sit here. There were problems every day. Every day was a new drama that had to be dealt with. We had to cooperate with the police and the army. That's why this event -- I'm not minimising this event and its importance, but this all lasted far too long and we were all exhausted. And if we were to do an analysis, I'm still claiming that, in those times, where there was sadness all around, Srbac was the place with the least number of tragedies. This is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I understand very well. I hear you. But I was under the impression that since yesterday you were attempting to tell us that you lived in a quiet and peaceful community in which not too many tragedies occurred. I was under the impression that you did not know -- that you didn't want to know what was going on around you, because in Srbac you were able to avoid all these stories, tragedies, and all of a sudden I seem to hear you say -- I hear you say that there were a lot of tragedies in Srbac as well. I am lost. I'm quite lost. I do not understand your testimony anymore. Could you please tell us, as the head of a community, what really happened. You're not here to play a cat and mouse game. We are asking you to tell us what happened in Srbac. Can you not give us the chronology of the events, in hindsight? Can you not tell us what happened exactly in Srbac? I would like to remind you that you are before a Tribunal and that this Tribunal is seeking to establish the truth. Judges would like to understand and hear the truth. You are here to tell us what happened the way you saw it, period. That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've been waiting for this answer, at least I'm speaking. As far as I'm concerned, I've been waiting for that answer since yesterday. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The municipality of Srbac, as I've told you, had 22.000 inhabitants, more or less. Out of them, there were 90-plus per cent Serbs. I told you how many Muslim families there were, how many Croats, and others. When the war started, we did not have so much tension, because of the figures, because of the ratio, and our goal was to prevent accidents among the three peoples. However, refugees came from Croatia, from Western Slavonia. They all came to Srbac. From Mrkonjic Grad -- when Mrkonjic Grad fell, Srbac was designated as the place where several thousand refugees would be accommodated in private houses, schools, and elsewhere. A lot of Croats and Serbs who went through Derventa had to pass through all this turmoil and contact. There were other peoples who passed through Srbac during the night. We didn't know who they were. And accidents could happen. However, I claim that we did our utmost to put a stop to such accidents and uncontrolled theft, murder, plunder, and killings. When soldiers came back home on leave, with arms, that was another story and a special problem. People would start getting relaxed. They would have a few drinks and started using weapons randomly. Sometimes those weapons were pointed at Serbs. Serbs also got killed. These people in Kobas were victims. At that time, the situation was very difficult. Even if you were too eager in dealing with the situation, then you could provoke those people who were on the front lines, who could hold that against you. However, given the circumstances, the geographical position, I can still say that we had a lot less problems in Srbac than in other municipalities. I don't know whether my answer satisfies you. I just tried to portray the situation in very brief outlines as it was in Srbac at the time. And that is why our efforts have been recognised by all those who are familiar with the essence of all these conflicts in that area, despite the victims. And now, when the Prosecutor asked me about the event in Banja Luka and big speeches, I just ignored him. I went back to Srbac and I dedicated my time to the problems in Srbac. I wanted to protect my municipality from any risks. When 22.000 refugees, Croats and Muslims, had to pass through Srbac on the way to Croatia, because we had good relations with Croatia, the situation was particularly tense and there was a danger that there would be a confrontation between the refugee Serbs who were in Srbac and those who were retreating towards Croatia, Muslims and Croats on their way to Croatia. In that, we played a role for which Mr. Komarica gave us credit, as well as the Croatian media, the Croatian side in general. Maybe this may not be in very good taste what I'm telling you now, but this is what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's just complete the Stankovic story before we move on. In fact, the killing of those two Muslim people and the shooting of two others on August 7th wasn't the end of Mr. Stankovic's activities, was it? Because, as this judgement indicates, Mr. Milincic, somehow he was released again. And in September of 1994 -- I see you shrugging your shoulder, like, what could you do, and we'll talk about that in a moment, but I want to note that for the record. In September of 1994, he shot two people again. In that instance, two Serb children, also from Srbac. You knew about that incident too, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed in writing. In the morning, I received a report on what had happened, and then I said, "People, can you save us from this man? Can somebody put an end to what he's doing, the violence that he's responsible for?" And it is very unfortunate that the president of the municipality had to launch an appeal of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you were shrugging your shoulders as I asked you the question, as if to say, "What could I do if the military authorities released this guy to be free again?" Was that what you were trying to say? And now I hear you whispering "yes," is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's try to recap the Stankovic story, then, if we can. In May of 1992, he murdered Mr. Hadziselimovic. In August of 1992, he murdered Hazim Zukanovic and --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was Hasima, a lady. Her name was Hasima.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And Reuf Alagic, and shot and seriously injured Hamza Bojadzic and Sabra Alagic, Reuf's mother. And then in September of 1994, free again, he shot two Serb children, and then was finally put in prison until approximately 2002. That's all correct; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you have just reminded me of the Serbian children. I have completely forgotten about them, unfortunately. It is correct what you have just said. That detail, unfortunately, has escaped me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And yet, Mr. Milincic, you came to this Court and you showed the Judges the partial documentation about Mr. Stankovic in order to convince them that in Srbac, and presumably in other parts of Republika Srpska, that if Muslims were attacked by Serbs, that the justice system took care of it. That was the wrong thing to do, wasn't it, Mr. Milincic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The system was not efficient; that is correct. But I have brought proof and I have tried to show you how the civilian bodies could not defend themselves from this pest that always accompanies a war. I didn't want to deceive you. My documentation is not complete. You have supplemented it. But my intention was to show you that there were killings, that there were accidents, and that people were put on trial. The efficiency of the system is a different story. This was beyond the scope of authority of the civilian bodies in Srbac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milincic. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I think the matter is relatively clear, where you said you brought documents to -- I think I summarised it even, to make sure that everything was done to prosecute people, that it was -- it's now that you say that you wanted to demonstrate that the civilian authorities were not responsible for the failure of the judicial authorities, which is, of course, quite a different message. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, far be it to come to Mr. Tieger's rescue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.
