utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But Mr. Tieger puts a serious allegation to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And with respect, I agree with Mr. Tieger. He needs to answer the question. I think Mr. Tieger was going to try again. And the reason I rise to my feet is Mr. Tieger's last question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- actually contains two questions and I would invite my learned friend to put the allegation to the witness, namely, he had come here to avoid telling the truth. I mean, there really is no point beating about the bush, in my submission, and to be fair to my learned friend, he's not attempting to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness told us several times that he came here to tell the truth, and unfortunately we had to establish that it was not in every way the full truth, the whole of the truth, and at the same time, we also have to notice that even today the reasons he gave for bringing these specific documents turn out to be slightly different reasons at the end of his testimony. I mean, it doesn't need, as far as we are concerned, it doesn't need much more attention. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, in fact, the reason you proactively set out to obtain partial documentation to prove -- in an attempt to prove certain points to the Court is because you believe that the actions taken in 1992 by the Bosnian Serb political and military authorities were appropriate in the defence of the Serbian people; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking about Srbac or in general? I'm not sure about the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me put it in a slightly different way. You don't have any quarrel with the use of illegal activity if you believe it to be in defence of the Serb people, and, in fact, have advocated illegal activity in the defence of the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "illegal activities in order to defend the Serb people." And again, I'm not clear. What specific activities pertaining to the defence of the Serb people? I'm not clear about the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Fine. How about this. How about this proposition. Let's take UN peacekeeping forces hostage in order to use them as a bargaining chip against the international community. That's something illegal and that's something you advocated, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps in a moment of desperation one can say anything, but there are limits to which we can go in order to defend ourselves or do things. I recall an event concerning an arrest of a UN representative. At the moment, amongst the public, amongst the people, it seemed to be a wise act. Later on, it turned out to be unwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A wise act. Well, let's look first at your comments on the 24th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly in January of 1993. We had an opportunity to look briefly at that earlier and I told you we'd be returning to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's tab 3, Your Honour, previous Exhibit P65, binder 15, tab 218. And Mr. Milincic's comments begin at the English on page 68. The relevant portion can be found on page 69.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Milincic, in B/C/S, that can be found at page 21, ERN 02149925. And at that time you said: "We too have something to blackmail them with. Khomeini in his time held a very small number of Americans in the American embassy in Tehran, and he sure did shake America quite well. Well, we also have enough of those white men," possibly men in white, "or others, and that could be some sort of a weapon. You know, we must somehow rebel against history. That is some kind of wisdom as well. Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, it seemed a logical thing to say. Today I wouldn't utter such words, but at that time I thought it wise. The only thing we could have done at that time, to address the events, was perhaps to do this, but fortunately it all ended well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A lot of things were seen as wise at that time in order to defend the Serb people in the eyes of the Bosnian Serb leadership that don't seem wise in retrospect; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, at that moment, things seemed that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Milincic, the reason -- or among the reasons, at any rate, that you offered a favourable and positive assessment of Mr. Krajisnik's character, when asked by the Defence, was because you believe he feels the same way as you do; that is, that many actions are permissible, including illegal actions, in the defence of the Serb people. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to repeat your question, because I better be very cautious when providing answers. Could you please repeat the question. I'm not trying to provoke, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, it is a type of question which easily results in debate rather than in witness testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'll just break it down, if I may, to at least some more elementary steps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understood you in response to questions asked by the Defence to be offering a favourable assessment, evaluation, opinion, of Mr. Krajisnik's character. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm suggesting you to you that the reason behind that opinion is that you believe him to share your attitudes, some of which you've just expressed, toward defending the Serb people, and so you want to say something favourable about him in court for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The knowledge I possess about Mr. Krajisnik, in the direction of the fact that in Srbac I have never received either an oral or a written directive from him pertaining to ethnic cleansing. Anything further than that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You did offer an opinion beyond that, and you offered us a favourable view of his character. And you were asked specifically about his character. Let me give you a more concrete example. You've just testified that you advocated the illegal activity of taking hostages. Now, part of the reason, I submit to you, that you're here offering favourable testimony to the extent you can, on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik, is because you know that he advocated the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't respond with a yes or no, but I do not agree with the way you formulated the question and with your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to play you two intercepts and then ask -- re-ask you -- or ask you a question. And the first one is found at tab 9, and it's ETRR 012680.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, just for housekeeping, I should probably get an exhibit number for this and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And apart from that, do the interpreters have a transcript? Because I didn't -- the interpreters need to have a transcript, because following the speed of the speech is -- it's tab 9 in the bundle, and meanwhile, Mr. Registrar could assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P988, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P988. And then I think that's the audio. And then P P988 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: ".A" would be the B/C/S transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The B/C/S transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P988A.1 would be the English translation of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, everyone has the copy in front of him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: MX: Hi there, namesake. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Hi there, namesake. MX: How are you? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Like king Milan Obrenovic. MX: You're better than he was. You're working professionally like doctors, you have the entire western world in mourning. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, right. So is there any news. MX: This is what there is. I think that you're doing things very well. This is the right way, because this hurts the most. You see, the English have now gone to see Milosevic and are forcing him to recognise Bosnia with the borders determined by the Avnoj Anti-fascist Council of the National Liberation of Yugoslavia. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Who went there? MX: The English. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Who from the English? MX: I don't know. I've just received a message from Chicago that the English have gone to Belgrade. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Uh-huh. To recognise ... MX: Yes, to recognise Bosnia with the borders determined by the Avnoj. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: So what do the English want? MX: Well, they want to put the pressure on you. They want to isolate and demoralise you completely. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: They can't do either of the two. We've become immune to that. MX: Well, I know that, but they don't. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I don't know how to explain it to them. MX: You can't. They are stupid. It's a stupid nation. The Anglo-Saxon brain is one with very limited abilities. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: So what are you, the Serbs in the West, doing? Why don't you give them a hint about what they should do? MX: We don't want to teach them about how it's done. We're teaching you. We are telling you what Anglo-Saxon brains are like because you don't know them and we know them inside out. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Right. MX: Look, this thing that you're doing is ingenious, absolutely. They have no options and they are constantly meeting. Kozirjev has called you barbarians. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Kozirjev? MX: Yes. He says that you are barbarians because you tied the Blue Helmets to the bridges, et cetera. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Kozirjev? And we received some information that he defended us. MX: Come on, he didn't defend you. Don't you believe that. He's a piece of garbage. He's a Jew before he's a Slav. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I know that. MX: Look, the best ... It is ugly that there are 2.000 amphibious troops on that American aeroplane. The English have deployed 1.500 of their commandos. The French have deployed commandos as well. They are putting psychological pressure on you, as if they were trying to get the hostages out. You have to be prepared ... they are ... Die Welt, the German paper, has published an article saying that they have learnt from an unnamed source that if there is a rescue mission, it will be done by helicopters at night. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: We've received that information. We have that. MX: All right. So you have that. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: We know everything. They can continue. We'll prepare that ... MX: Look, there's another thing. Look, when you told me about the two to three thousand, that's a very good number if it can be done. It's a bit big, but it's very good, because you're spoiling their affairs. Neither can they rescue them in such a mission, nor can they bring NATO troops to Bosnia to evacuate the UNPROFOR, since you're holding 3.000 UNPROFOR members as hostages. Therefore, neither the first nor the second idea is an option. All they can do is agree to your conditions. You should negotiate everything, the territories, peace, anything, just not the hostages. The holding of hostages is a new way of waging war. You hold hostages as protection. Don't believe any promises. They have lied before; they'll lie again. Therefore, the hostages are a guarantee. Someone's word is no guarantee. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, yes, I understand that. That's what we'll do. MX: You have no other choice. You're in a situation where you can't do anything else. If you release them ... this time they've decided to regroup them and put them all on Muslim territory. They will give you all the enclaves in the east, Gorazde, Srebrenica, and Zepa, but when they arrive on Muslim territory, then the Muslims will constantly attack you. If you launch a counter-attack, they will bomb because you'll be attacking the UNPROFOR. Therefore, they have chosen a different tactic, so you mustn't let the hostages go anywhere, because you won't be able to catch them again. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Whom mustn't we release? MX: The hostages. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, yes. MX: Because you won't have a chance to catch them later and there won't be anyone to defend you from the bombardment. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, yes. MX: This is do or die moment for you. That's my opinion. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Good. That's it. MX: Tell me how we stand in other places. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Look, there's a great offensive. MX: Theirs? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, yes. MX: Where are they attacking us? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: On mount Ozren, in Bihac, everywhere. MX: I heard that we've won back what we'd lost in Bihac. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, we have, some of it. MX: Not everything? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: We've won back some of it and that's good. MX: I heard that your commander-in-chief has high blood problem. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Says who? MX: Well, he's at the VMA military medical academy. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, yes, it's a small problem, but he's fit as a fiddle. MX: Fit as a fiddle. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, yes. MX: It would be better if he were fit in the head. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Right. We're a strange people. We're all similar to each other. MX: Who's that that laughed there? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: It's me and my brother, nobody else. MX: Ah, you have a brother. I didn't know that. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, his name is Mirko. He's here to see me. We're watching something and I'm talking with you. MX: I saw a tied-up UNPROFOR coward. They asked him how they were being treated. He said very well, that they were taken to sleep at night and then brought back during the day. In fact, he told NATO that the targets were unprotected at night and that they could strike. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, yes, but tomorrow we'll ... MX: Look, put them into eight-hour shifts. They are rotten. They have very good devices for night-time bombardment. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Good. I think that they saw clearly what would happen to them, so they have to take care. MX: Look, they are counting on you giving in. Don't give in, because you'll lose a lot later. This time you have to be strong right to the end. I don't see any other way of dealing with them, because if Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you're strong first and then give in, they won't take you seriously. I heard Douglas Herd a journalist. I asked him, "I hear that Mr. Karadzic said that he would kill one UN soldier after each bomb that fell." He replied that Mr. Karadzic had spoken rubbish earlier as well and that it wasn't important what he said but what he did. Therefore, don't give statements if you don't plan to follow them. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: That's right. I absolutely agree. MX: Say only what you're going to do and if you're able to do it. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I absolutely agree. MX: They appreciate only that. They only respect a firm opinion and not softies. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, yes, I absolute agree. MX: You have to be very good there. I know that it's not easy. It's easy for me for speak about it from here. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: If nothing else, I respect that, my man. If you only knew what a great thing it is that you sympathise with us. You can't wage war here in our place. We give all this very high marks. If only you knew what would happen were it not for our people. MX: It's a bit easier like this, isn't it. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: By all means. In the biggest evil, it's a great thing when people find ... MX: And we tell you something that's important; right? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Of course. We very much respect that. MX: I'm very happy about that, because I really want to help. I want to see that first Serb state and then retire. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: There are only few such big Serbs in the world. MX: Create a state and then I can retire there. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: That's right. Good for us that we have such wonderful people. MX: Since I am a professor at university, I'll go to Banja Luka and establish a university there. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: It will be in Sarajevo as well. MX: Forget about Sarajevo. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: We want it there, where it's a bit harder for us. It's easy to do there. MX: We'll have to chase all the Mujos out, all the Turks. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: There are no -- there are no Muslims here in our part. MX: Forget about our part, man. The entire Sarajevo will be ours or ... forget about our part. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: No division, huh? MX: A lawyer called Di Maggio, specialising in international law, is giving a lecture here and he's talking about the Balkan conflict and he says that there are Bosnians, Serbs, and Croats there. So I asked him who the Bosnians were and he said it was the Muslims. I told him that the Serbs and Croats were Bosnians as well. He told me that the Serbs have Serbs across the Drina and the Croats have Croats on the other side, but the Muslims don't know where to hit. I replied that they didn't know where to hit because they are not a nation. I told him that they wanted to impose a group of people that are not a nation to rule over two nations. That cannot be. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: That's exactly so, and it's a disaster that people don't know about it. MX: It's not a nation. It's Serbs and Croats who converted to Islam, nothing more. Renegades. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Exactly, but God forbid, they are not our people and we should split up. MX: Look, at this moment we need to split up. I am certain that we'll be joint again in a hundred years, but right now it's impossible. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: With whom? MX: With the Turks. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: There's no way that we'll be joint with them. MX: In a hundred years we will be joint economically, but now, no way. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: We will never be joint with them. We'll curse all our generations if they join them. MX: Then let's do it like that. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Why would we join them? What do we need them for? Only if they convert to another faith. MX: That's right. They can become Orthodox again. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: That's right. MX: What's the situation near Orasje? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: There's a big offensive, today and this morning. MX: Is that so? Are we holding out well? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: We are, my man. I'll talk to you tomorrow. MX: All the best. I'll talk to you. Give my regards to Radovan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the next one will be quite brief. It's a conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Slobodan Stupar, on 28 May, 1992, found in the same tab -- excuse me. Found at tab 8, and it needs a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P989, Your Honours. The transcript will be P989.A, and the translation will be P989A.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is, as I indicated, a conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Stupar for a news programme, and the short clip begins at page 2 of the English translation, with a comment by Mr. Stupar, Mr. Krajisnik. According to news agencies, Mr. Chirac talked to the president of Serbia. STUPAR: Mr. Krajisnik, according to news agencies, Mr. Chirac talked to the president of Serbia, Mr. Milosevic, today. He asked him to use his authority and try to reach an agreement to release the UNPROFOR soldiers. What is your comment on that conversation and the ability of the president of Serbia to mediate in the present situation? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: No heavy price. President Milosevic demands and no divisions can make us not respect the president of our mother state. But we are dealing with dirty tricks here. All the resolutions that the foreign powers wanted to impose, they imposed through the French. It is particularly the French side which shows no intention of helping us. We regret that they are innocent guys, but we have to treat the United Nations the way they deserve. The thing is, the UN has sided with our enemy, and we have to ... because it cannot be a Serb is a lesser being, whether he is a soldier or a civilian. If he is defending his home and his freedom and if he is clearly not an aggressor on his own territory. The UN and NATO are aggressors, and they have shown their true colours. All their policies were directed against the Serbs, and we put up with it in order to realise our just goals. In connection with the events in Western Slavonia, and after the events in the safe areas, which are in fact unprotected areas with civilians, but also in view of the armed forces positions which keep attacking our territory, the UN has lost the minimum of respect and trust the Serbs should have towards them, which we tried to instil in our people. "The UN has in fact, through NATO, committed a crime against our people, and that is why the only solution is for the war to stop and for peace to be introduced in this area. Those who have ordered the bombardment do not want peace; they just generated an escalation of the conflict. "I do not want to jump to conclusions. Everything is possible in diplomacy. We shall do our best to show flexibility and cooperativeness, but we shall no longer allow the international mediators to bring us in the situation such as at the 31 December, when we accepted a cease-fire, which was then used to arm the Muslim army, while nothing has been done to change the public position of America, which says that they just want to hear clearly that the Serbian side accepts the Contact Group plan, which has clearly shown that it is an unjust solution and that one side in the conflict is totally against it and doesn't accept it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, for the previous intercept, do we have any more information about the other interlocutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not at this moment, Your Honour, but I will -- I think -- well, I'll pursue that and I think we may be able to obtain further information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- that would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, I'll put it to you simply. You and Mr. Krajisnik share views about doing what is seen as necessary, even if it's illegal, to defend the Serbs, and that's at least part of the reason why you proactively sought out partial documentation to assist him here in court. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My information is what it is. I offered it to you, but not only to help Krajisnik, but also to help finding the truth. And the truth is that in the municipality of Srbac and the situation that was there and the influence of Krajisnik on the Serbs in the Srbac municipality. This is the only thing I can tell you. What I have brought is just an attempt for us to -- for you to understand what circumstances we were in, that we were equally safe or equally threatened, both Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to seek a clarification on the last answer you gave. You said that you -- "the truth is that in the municipality of Srbac and the situation that was there and the influence of Krajisnik on the Serbs in the Srbac municipality." What did you have in mind when you said "the influence of Krajisnik on the Serbs in the Srbac municipality"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I saw Krajisnik in passing, when this was not planned at a celebration or at a meeting, he would always ask me how things were. He asked me to try and protect peace, to protect Muslims and Croats, because he said, "If you are threatened by them, then you are no Serbs at all." There were no other negative influences. He never said anything negative. He always told me, "You are easy to deal with, because you never have problems there."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Josse, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or would you rather first have a break? We could now take the break of 20 minutes and then restart at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I avail myself of that offer? But before the break, perhaps I could address the Chamber in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milincic, we will have a break after Mr. Josse has addressed the Chamber on what seems to be a procedural matter. Could you please follow Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate that I need to conduct my case as I see fit, but I also appreciate that this Chamber, quite properly, takes a proactive role in the receipt of evidence. I deliberately didn't deal with the last tab in the bundle that I had -- the Defence had prepared for this witness. It's part of an article from a Croatian magazine which, in essence, as I understand it - it's not been translated, of course - praises inter-ethnic relations between Srbac municipality and the municipality across the river Sava, in about 1995. And really, I deliberately wanted to wait to see the extent to which my learned friend attacked the witness. Bearing in mind what he's been asked, I am inclined to try and adduce that document in the course of re-examination. However, I don't want to spend a lot of time on it, if you and your colleagues take the view that really it wouldn't add anything very much to his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, we do not know. First of all, we haven't read it either, so it might well be that it adds to what you would consider the proper balance between the issues dealt with in cross-examination and then examination-in-chief, in view of the development of the examination of this witness, including cross-examination. I would not prevent you from doing it. I think it's fair, although usually we expect the parties to exhaust, to the best of their abilities, the evidence in the examination-in-chief, of course. But I do understand under the present circumstances where you might not have found time, but you have prioritised in a different way --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. It wasn't even so much that. It was in my mind that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you find it important, if you find it important.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It depended on the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually I would not reserve elements of the evidence to see whether or not to use them after we heard what the cross-examination is about. I mean, that would be the proper -- the -- an improper approach, I would say, because then cross-examination would be a kind of a try-out of what --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But at the same time, we noticed that this is not your strategy or not your usual approach. And I also do understand that the development of the testimony of this witness might have -- might not have been exactly what you expected from the witness. So therefore, I would allow you to do it. One advice: Please read it carefully, because -- before you ask any questions to the witness about it, because it seems that -- let's just take the issue of prosecution and sentence. Of course, one of the first things that came into my mind, how do we identify what murder is dealt with in this judgement. Of course, I can imagine, especially if you have received the document only recently, that it brings you some surprises as well. So therefore, my advice is to take care that you have seen every single part of it. Apart from that, would you need additional time with Mr. Krajisnik? I mean, how -- usually second break is 20 minutes. If you apply for 30 -- I'd like, to the extent possible, to finish with the witness today. The Judges have already put a lot of questions to the witness, so there might not be many left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I could have 30, I would again accept that offer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll try to finish with the witness today, and we'll have a break of 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution have chosen to play this very long intercept and ask about one question at the end of it. I intend to re-examine the witness extensively about the intercept, if Your Honours will permit me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you are allowed to do that. But I take it that we remain approximately within the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then the witness may be brought into the courtroom. I take it that you have no further issues, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, you'll be re-examined by Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, I'd like to begin my re-examination by putting to you in part the very last question that my learned friend Mr. Tieger, on behalf of the Prosecution, asked you. And I'm going to begin at the end of the question. The end of the question was that you proactively sought out partial documentation to assist Mr. Krajisnik here in Court. Is there any truth in that allegation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed that I should bring some documents to demonstrate what circumstances we worked and lived under in Srbac during the war, that we were not spared, none of us, and that we were not safe, none of us. And this is what I have attempted to illustrate with the papers, showing that there were Muslims in the Serbian army, that they had rights, and how they exercised them. As for the killings, unfortunately, I ignored two more killings. But I also ignored the killings of two Serbs. But this is what happened during the war. It was not my intention to mislead anybody or to create a false impression of an idyll in Srbac. We tried to cope with problems as best we could, and those problems arose from the war, even in an area such was Srbac at the time. My powers, or lack of them, as a civilian president, in order to protect the interests of the three sides, are also illustrated by that. The general impression of the general public, bearing in mind the circumstances that we lived in, shows that Srbac was successful in maintaining order, and of course we regret the victims that we still had, despite our efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, could I echo what, in particular, the learned Judge, Judge Hanoteau, has said to you. Listen to the question that I'm asking you. You've given a long explanation, which you have given to this Court before. I want you to focus on the question that you're being asked. I'll repeat my question once again. It was suggested to you that you proactively sought out partial documentation to assist Mr. Krajisnik here in Court. Do you understand that question?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the question. But that was not my intention. I did not want to propose partial documents, biased documents, in order to help Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it was further suggested to you that you and Mr. Krajisnik share views about doing illegal things. Do you believe in doing illegal things?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't think that anybody should do illegal things. But I also believe that, based on one sentence that I uttered there, about hostages, I believe, one shouldn't conclude that we support lawlessness. On the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you recall Mr. Krajisnik ever publicly advocating illegal things?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the intercept that I heard here, I concluded that there is a story there that could be interpreted in one way or in another, and my information, the information that I received in my municipality, do not confirm that he ever asked for illegal things to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, just -- we are not a jury; we are Judges with some experience. We'd be greatly surprised if a witness, especially after hearing the whole of his testimony, would answer to your question whether he would share an intent with Mr. Krajisnik to do illegal things."Yes, of course, I do share ..." I mean, we are good enough observers from the testimony. The witness explained what he did, under what circumstances he did it. At the same time, we have heard what he said in the assembly. So all together, we are perfectly able to make up our minds. And I don't think -- perhaps for a jury it would make a difference, but, really, to seek confirmation with question: "Did you come here with the intent ..." It's clear what the witness did. The witness I think feared that there might be an unbalanced view on what happened and very much was eager to not let it happen that after his testimony there would still be such an unbalanced -- and therefore he may have sought to bring some material which, in his view, completed the picture, which is, of course, not very wise for a witness to do, because he has got no idea what our picture is until now; he hasn't heard the evidence. Therefore, I already more or less said to Mr. Tieger at an earlier stage whether we'd need certain types of questions. He continued them, as a matter of fact. I say the same to you, and I think it's -- I hope you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do. I'm going to move on. It may be a subject I'd like to return to when we've a little bit more time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The intercept, Mr. Milincic, 29th of May of 1995, what was happening in the Republic of Srpska in relation to NATO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I think there would be no problem if there was some leading on these events. I mean that there were specific type of problems, I mean, is so widely known, I would say, that eliciting from the witness this in the traditional, non-leading way is not really necessary. But Mr. Tieger certainly will object if he thinks that leading goes too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: NATO was bombing, in part, the Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That bombing was directed against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Serbs living in the Republika Srpska were very upset?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And would you accept that the conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. X had that backdrop, the backdrop of the bombing, to put it into some sort of context?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The content of the conversation points to that. This X suggests things from a distance. He is safe and he tells us what we were supposed to do here. I was always against those advisors who provide advice from a distance. This conversation was, as you've heard, full of suggestions for us to do what they think we should do, from their safe position.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just help me, and indeed the Chamber: How were you able to glean from the conversation that X was at a safe distance? What was it that he said that made you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He says, "I'm going to come and establish a university in Banja Luka," which clearly shows that he is not here. I don't know where he is. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. We first have to survive, to save our hide, the area, schools, houses, roads. He mentions the next hundred years or so. It is just romantic stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the witness have a look, please, at tab 14 of the Defence documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you dealt with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- telephone conversation? Then I would have one additional question to you. Part of the conversation is: "I saw a tied-up UNPROFOR coward. They asked him how they were being treated. He said, Very well, that they were taken to sleep at night and then brought back during the day. In fact, he told NATO that the targets were unprotected at night and that they could strike." And then Mr. Krajisnik says: "Yes, yes, but tomorrow we'll ..." And then this person says: "Look, put them into eight-hour shifts. They're rotten. They have very good devices for night-time bombardment." "Tied-up UNPROFOR coward," do I have to understand that they were tied up to targets which could be bombed by NATO in order to prevent them from further doing that, and that in order to prevent that it happened at night, that they would put them on the eight-hour shifts, including the night? Is that a correct understanding of ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I watched those scenes on TV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I read this, and it came into my mind that people were tied to targets, well, possible targets for bombardment. Is that a correct understanding, in your view, of what is said here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so. I believe that they were target-oriented. It was about some facilities that had to be protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. By tying UNPROFOR hostages to those objects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tab 14, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is a copy of an article that you brought with you; is that correct, Mr. Milincic? Just yes or no, because I want to lead you through some of this, because it will make it much easier.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have brought this as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And indeed, you have still in your possession the original of this. It's from a colour magazine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a Croatian weekly called Arena, published in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And how did it come into your possession, the magazine, that is?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People from Croatia sent this to me when it was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you any idea when it was published?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995, in late 1995, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, we are again suffering from the same handicap of not having a translation. What I want you to do, briefly if you can, is to summarise what you understand this article to be saying.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995, when the so-called Autonomous Region of Krajina fell, after the Bljesak and Oluja operations of the Croatian Armed Forces, and as the Serbs were fleeing towards these areas of Republika Srpska, and this is what the article is all about. The Bosniaks and Croats started withdrawing from those areas because they feared a retaliation by the Serbs who were fleeing the Croatian Armed Forces and arriving in Bosnia and Herzegovina, i.e., Republika Srpska. Based on previous agreements between the vice-president of Republika Srpska, Dr. Nikola Koljevic, and the representative of the International Red Cross, Sommaruga, which were struck in either 1992 or 1993, Srbac was designated as a place which was safer and more secure than other municipalities to be like a customs zone or a no man's zone, where the families could find shelter and get connected and reunited. We had Serb families moving towards Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as Croats and Muslims who were crossing the Sava near Srbac to go on to the river Sava, to a place called Davor. In 1995, which is the year that this article writes about, when these things were happening in Croatia and when the Croatian army liberated the area that I have mentioned, and when the AR Krajina disappeared, and when numerous Serbs had been pushed and thus jeopardised the Muslims and Croats, the Muslims and Croats crossed the Sava to go to Croatia, near the place called Davor. This was a dramatic period, because 22.000 Bosniaks and Croats from various municipalities of Krajina across Srbac were transported in various vehicles, lorries and so on and so forth. This was done in an organised manner. And they crossed the Savo to go into Croatia. This article describes that period and describes a man who is calling across from the river Sava, giving a message from the president of the municipality of Davor to the president of the municipality of Srbac, asking the two of them to meet and to organise this crossing in the safest possible manner. This article also brings the story of individuals, Croats and Muslims, the tragic stories of those who crossed into Croatia and what happened to them there. The point here is that it is only a fortunate thing that there was such two places as Srbac and Davor, where people could find shelter for a while until the political situation was resolved on both sides. And when people returned to their homes, the Srbac municipality received a lot of thank-you notes, which, in the general atmosphere of catastrophe, offered help to these people. And I may be repeating myself when I say that about a month ago, in Banja Luka, the Croatian grammar school was opened in Banja Luka. The Banja Luka bishop approached me on that occasion and thanked me for everything that we had done in those hard times. He knew what the situation was like, and this article is but a fragment of the overall picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It mentions you in a number of places. I think it states that you were in fact educated, in part, in Zagreb. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a mistake. I have a lot of students, former students, in Croatia. I graduated from the University of Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it generally talks about your role as president of the municipality in the events that you've just described; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll submit that for translation, and could that be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D102, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have nothing else. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Nothing arises, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noticed that from different parts of your testimony, it appears that Kobas was a mainly Muslim village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although there were quite a number of Serbs living there as well, let's say up to perhaps 10 per cent?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is the so-called Kobas centre, and there is also a periphery, and Bosniaks are mostly in the centre. And in the peripheral part, there are also Serbs. The population is somewhat mixed, but the centre is mostly composed of Muslims, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are the Muslims and the Serbs who used to live in Kobas, are they still living together in that area? Because I noticed that on the list of candidates, some candidates, mainly not of SDS or SDA, that they are Serbs but living in Kobas. I noticed that this is for Mile Majdanac. I don't know whether the name is familiar to you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is true for Aleksandar Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He died. I used to know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for Milanko Dzekic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do they still live there? Of course, I do understand that Mr. Nikolic died. Did he die during the war or after the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: During the war. The other two persons, are they still living there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, they do. If they're still alive, yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the Muslims that were living in Kobas, does the majority of those who lived there at the beginning of the war still there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kobas?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 69 families left during the war from Kobas, and refugees from Vozic [phoen], near Doboj, moved from their houses, the Serb refugees. After the war the situation was reinstated. I believe that everybody returned but the young ones, who decided not to go back home, whereas the older people returned to their homes. The person who is in charge of that in the municipality, who is in charge of the restoration of property, left his job. Actually, lost his job. Once the property issues were resolved, the office was closed down and that person had nothing left to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean that those who left their property either got it back or were compensated, or is there anyone who is not, or not, fully compensated for property they left behind?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in the Srbac municipality for long, but according to most of the information I received, a lot of people returned, and they all moved back into their houses. And whether some houses were damaged or not, I don't know, but I believe they all returned to their properties. And to add: A new mosque was built. It wasn't restored, but rather a completely new one was built in Kobas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But do I have to understand your testimony to be that every Muslim house that was still there after the war was again occupied by its original owners?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I left for The Hague, before that, I went to see the current municipal president in Srbac, as well as the assembly president, and I told them I was to go to The Hague and that I had to obtain some information as to what was happening. I asked to see the papers that I brought, and I asked them about Kobas, whether things were okay over there. And they said all the people returned to their property and there are no outstanding issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no personal knowledge of it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the last two days learned us to be very cautious at least before accepting information you received before leaving to The Hague. I have no further questions. Any need arisen from the questions of the Bench? Then, Mr. Milincic, this concludes your testimony in this Court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and to answer the questions of both parties and of the Bench. We appreciate it, that you were willing to come, and we wish you a safe trip home again. Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Milincic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any other procedural matter at this moment, apart from --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Josse, do you have any information now on the witness which is expected to appear on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. It's a very regrettable state of affairs. We will know tomorrow morning, so I am told, whether he will have a visa to enable him to travel to this country over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, I'm not in a position to urge my government to issue visas, because I've got nothing to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, it's not a fault of your government, Your Honour. Let me make that quite clear. And it's not the fault of the VWS. Let me make that also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not going to inquire any further into whose fault it is, but it sounds a bit as coming close to miracle. We'll then adjourn until next Monday, unless we receive information about the witness not being able to travel to The Hague. And then instructions will follow whether we would nevertheless be in Court next Monday afternoon, perhaps for other reasons, or whether we would just wait until the witness is available to be examined. So therefore, provisionally, we adjourn until Monday, the 14th of November, Courtroom I, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
